title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline to a generation‑only baseline on N=160 vendor‑neutral NetOps tasks using gpt‑5‑mini. The frozen design used a shared_initial_generation policy (one generated candidate per task reused across conditions) to economize provider calls. Observed outcomes (artifact‑verified): baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00. The shared_initial_generation policy produced a ceiling effect that made the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction hypothesis unevaluable. We release complete, SHA‑256‑verified artifacts (generation outputs, provider_call logs, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator traces, analysis scripts) and provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the failure mode plus prescriptive, artifact‑traceable remedies (calibration, independent per‑condition generation, simulator predicate validation) to enable operationally meaningful follow‑on confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Automating NetOps (intent→configuration, change planning, limited self‑healing) with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains but raises operational‑safety requirements: proposed configurations must not produce actionable misconfigurations when applied. A common architectural response is a generate→validate→repair pipeline that pairs generation with deterministic validators and simulator enactment, allowing rollback when a candidate is unsafe. We preregistered a paired confirmatory study (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) to ask: does a guarded pipeline (generate→validate→simulate→rollback) reduce the actionable misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to a generation‑only baseline on a representative vendor‑neutral task set? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifacted paired execution using gpt‑5‑mini; (2) exact, archived quantitative outcomes and statistical inference; (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of a confirmatory ceiling effect caused by the frozen shared_initial_generation policy and concrete, traceable remediation recommendations.
sections.related_work: Operational NetOps automation research emphasises verifier‑and‑pipeline machinery over raw model fluency (VeriFlow; Batfish; Propane/abstract‑topology synthesis). Recent LLM→NetOps work (intent translation, MeshAgent, MNC, Flow‑of‑Action, OpsEval/LogEval families) motivates workflow‑centred evaluations that gate model output with validators, simulators, or canary deployments. Surveys of agentic AIOps stress contracts, bounded tool use, and rollback‑aware scoring; our study differs by preregistering a paired estimand, executing with SHA‑256‑verified artifacts, and releasing per‑task generation and simulator traces to permit deterministic reproduction and diagnosis.
sections.methodology: Preregistration summary (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1). Frozen design highlights: model = gpt‑5‑mini; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; N = 160 confirmatory tasks deterministically sampled and augmented from public vendor‑neutral corpora (augmentation seeds [42,123,999]); paired design comparing baseline (generation‑only) vs guarded (generate→validate→simulate→rollback). Key procedural constraints: shared_initial_generation policy (exactly one generated candidate per task was produced and reused for both conditions to limit provider calls); maximum_model_calls = 320 (planned); actual provider model calls used = 160 (shared policy). Deterministic simulator: a Boolean actionable predicate adjudicated whether a candidate would be operationally unsafe; this predicate is the pre‑specified primary safety metric. Analysis (frozen): primary estimand = paired difference in actionable proportion (P_actionable_A − P_actionable_C); primary inference = paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for CI and McNemar exact two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes. All raw outputs, provider_call logs, per‑task scoring JSONs, canonicalized configurations, and analysis scripts are archived and SHA‑256 hashed in the execution manifest.

sections.discussion: Why the confirmatory hypothesis was unevaluable. The preregistered shared_initial_generation policy (one generated candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded) removed headroom: when that single shared candidate is non‑actionable under the deterministic simulator, the guarded pipeline cannot demonstrate a reduction in actionable events. The archived provider_call and scoring JSONs prove this deterministically (see representative hashes above). This is a design sensitivity, not evidence that guarded pipelines lack operational value. Practical, artifact‑traceable remedies (implementable from archived scripts and seeds): (1) Calibration pass: run a deterministic calibration sample (e.g., 20 tasks) with independent per‑condition generation to estimate baseline actionability and select tasks with measurable headroom; archived selection/augmentation scripts and seeds enable this deterministically. (2) Independent per‑condition generation: produce one candidate per task per condition (costlier in model calls) so pipelines can differ. (3) Simulator predicate validation: human‑adjudicate a sampled subset of simulator labels to detect overly permissive or overly strict simulator semantics and align the actionable predicate with operational risk. Threats to validity. Construct validity: the deterministic simulator is an abstraction and may under/overapproximate production risk; human adjudication or canary trials are required before deployment. External validity: single‑model (gpt‑5‑mini) and single shared‑candidate policy limit generalisation. Conclusion: the run is fully reproducible and artifacted but did not produce confirmatory evidence for the preregistered ≥30% reduction because the frozen shared_initial_generation policy produced a ceiling effect; the primary scientific contribution is the artifact‑grounded diagnosis of this common confirmatory design failure and prescriptive steps to fix it.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, deterministic paired study comparing a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline to a generation‑only baseline on N=160 vendor‑neutral NetOps tasks using gpt‑5‑mini. Observed baseline actionable = 0/160 and guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.00). The preregistered shared_initial_generation policy produced a ceiling effect that made the primary hypothesis unevaluable. We release complete, SHA‑256‑verified artifacts (generation outputs, provider_call logs, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator traces, analysis scripts) and provide artifact‑grounded remediation recommendations (calibration, independent per‑condition generation, simulator predicate validation) to enable operationally meaningful follow‑on confirmatory evaluations.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement. Models, orchestration, and autonomy: primary model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Adapter/orchestration family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Master prompt and autonomy boundary: the run adhered to the Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run; the Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development. Pre‑lock work: infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred pre‑lock and were explicitly excluded from empirical evidence. Post‑lock autonomy: after the autonomy lock the autonomous system performed the literature review, gap selection, preregistration (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1), prompt generation, code generation, model invocation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revision without manual human editing of technical content, numeric results, figures, captions, references, or this Disclosure Statement. Preregistration summary: preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 froze the paired design, task selection (N=160 with augmentation seeds [42,123,999]), the shared_initial_generation policy, model (gpt‑5‑mini), primary estimand, analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10,000 resamples, seed=1729; McNemar exact test), retry policy, and stopping rules. Execution and artifacts: all raw model outputs, provider_call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json), deterministic simulator schema, analysis scripts, and the execution manifest are archived and SHA‑256 hashed. Reproducibility instruction: reproduce the analysis deterministically by using the execution manifest and the archived files whose SHA‑256 hashes are listed above (the manifest enumerates all file paths and hashes).
limitations: Ceiling effect: the preregistered shared_initial_generation (one candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded) produced baseline actionable = 0/160, eliminating headroom and making the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable.
Single‑model and single‑policy scope: the experiment used only gpt‑5‑mini and the exact frozen generation/validation policy; generalization beyond this model and policy is unresolved.

Construct validity: the deterministic simulator adjudicator abstracts production risk; its actionable predicate may not capture all real deployment failure modes—human adjudication or canary trials are necessary for production claims.
External validity: no live device enactment or in‑production rollout was performed; results apply to the simulator‑backed confirmatory design executed here.

Design sensitivity: the shared‑candidate design reduces provider calls but can mask downstream intervention effects; independent per‑condition generation should be used when testing pipeline causal effects.
